Deuteronomy — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)

Deuteronomy repeats much of the history and many of the laws found in the preceding three books.

Moses delivered this teaching to Israel shortly before his death.

He spoke it aloud so that it would deeply affect the people, and he wrote it down so that it would remain with them.

The generation to whom the law was first given had died.

A new generation had taken its place, and God wanted Moses himself to repeat the law as they prepared to possess Canaan.

The book shows God's extraordinary love for his church.

For his own mercy's sake, he continually preserved his people and intended that his name should still be invoked among them.

The whole book also displays Moses' love for Israel and makes him a remarkable picture of the Lord Jesus Christ.

May we apply its appeals and encouragements to our own consciences, so that we are moved to grateful, believing obedience to God's commands.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe words Moses spake to Israel in the plains of Moab, The promise of Canaan.1–8Judges provided for the people.9–18Of the sending the spies—God's anger for their unbelief and disobedience.19–46
Moses reminds Israel of the command to enter Canaan (verses 1–8)

Moses told the people everything the Lord had commanded him to say.

Horeb was only eleven days' journey from Kadesh-barnea.

Remembering that distance would help Israel understand how much suffering their own disobedience had brought upon them.

They had wandered for years because they had refused to believe God.

This memory should encourage them to recognize the benefits of obedience.

Now the Lord commanded them to move forward.

Although he brings his people through hardship and testing, he also knows when they have suffered long enough.

When he commands us to advance in the Christian life, he places the heavenly Canaan before us to encourage us.

The appointment of judges (verses 9–18)

Moses reminded Israel of its well-ordered system of government.

If the people used it properly, the system could make life peaceful and secure.

He acknowledged that God had fulfilled the promise to multiply Abraham's descendants.

He also prayed that the Lord would continue fulfilling it.

God's goodness and power are not limited. Why should our faith and hope be limited?

The Lord had given Israel good laws and provided good people to administer them.

This showed both his care for Israel and the care Moses had taken for the people.

The spies and Israel's unbelief (verses 19–46)

Moses recalled the difficult journey from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea through the great and terrifying wilderness.

By then the people were very close to Canaan.

The final ruin of hypocrites will be made more terrible by the realization that they had once been not far from God's kingdom.

Israel had every assurance that its God would go ahead.

But the people still wanted to send men ahead to investigate the land.

Everyone who saw Canaan had to admit that it was good.

What reason, then, did Israel have to distrust the Lord who promised to give it to them?

Unbelief lay beneath their whole rebellion.

Every refusal to obey God's law and every suspicion of his power and goodness ultimately springs from disbelief of his word.

True obedience, by contrast, flows from faith.

We would benefit from dividing our past lives into distinct periods.

For each period, we should thank God for the mercies we received, confess the sins we remember and seek forgiveness.

In this way we can renew our acceptance of God's salvation and our dedication to his service.

Our independent plans rarely lead us to the best outcome.

But courage born of faith and expressed through duty enables believers to follow the Lord fully, stand firm against obstacles, triumph over opposition and take hold of the blessings he promises.
classic_reading:
[Deut.1.1-Deut.1.8]
Deuteronomy
This book repeats much of the history and of the laws contained in the three foregoing books: Moses delivered it to Israel a little before his death, both by word of mouth, that it might affect, and by writing, that it might abide. The men of that generation to which the law was first given were all dead, and a new generation was sprung up, to whom God would have it repeated by Moses himself, now they were going to possess the land of Canaan. The wonderful love of God to his church is set forth in this book; how he ever preserved his church for his own mercies sake, and would still have his name called upon among them. Such are the general outlines of this book, the whole of which shows Moses' love for Israel, and marks him an eminent type of the Lord Jesus Christ. Let us apply the exhortations and persuasions to our own consciences, to excite our minds to a believing, grateful obedience to the commands of God.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The words Moses spake to Israel in the plains of Moab, The promise of Canaan. | (1-8) |
Judges provided for the people. | (9-18) |
Of the sending the spies--God's anger for their unbelief and disobedience.
(19-46)
Verses 1-8
Moses spake to the people all the Lord had given him in commandment. Horeb was but eleven days distant from Kadesh-barnea. This was to remind them that their own bad conduct had occasioned their tedious wanderings; that they might the more readily understand the advantages of obedience. They must now go forward. Though God brings his people into trouble and affliction, he knows when they have been tried long enough. When God commands us to go forward in our Christian course, he sets the heavenly Canaan before us for our encouragement.
[Deut.1.9-Deut.1.18]
Verses 9-18
Moses reminds the people of the happy constitution of their government, which might make them all safe and easy, if it was not their own fault. He owns the fulfilment of God's promise to Abraham, and prays for the further accomplishment of it. We are not straitened in the power and goodness of God; why should we be straitened in our own faith and hope? Good laws were given to the Israelites, and good men were to see to the execution of them, which showed God's goodness to them, and the care of Moses.
[Deut.1.19-Deut.1.46]
Verses 19-46
Moses reminds the Israelites of their march from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea, through that great and terrible wilderness. He shows how near they were to a happy settlement in Canaan. It will aggravate the eternal ruin of hypocrites, that they were not far from the kingdom of God. As if it were not enough that they were sure of their God before them, they would send men before them. Never any looked into the Holy Land, but they must own it to be a good land. And was there any cause to distrust this God? An unbelieving heart was at the bottom of all this. All disobedience to God's laws, and distrust of his power and goodness, flow from disbelief of his word, as all true obedience springs from faith. It is profitable for us to divide our past lives into distinct periods; to give thanks to God for the mercies we have received in each, to confess and seek the forgiveness of all the sins we can remember; and thus to renew our acceptance of God's salvation, and our surrender of ourselves to his service. Our own plans seldom avail to good purpose; while courage in the exercise of faith, and in the path of duty, enables the believer to follow the Lord fully, to disregard all that opposes, to triumph over all opposition, and to take firm hold upon the promised blessings.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Edomites to be spared.1–7The Moabites and Ammonites to be spared.8–23The Amorites to be destroyed.24–37
Israel must not attack Edom (verses 1–7)

Moses gives only a brief account of Israel's many years in the wilderness.

God had corrected the people for complaining and unbelief.

But he was also preparing them for Canaan—humbling them over sin, teaching them to fight against sinful desires, follow him and find comfort in him.

God's people may wait a long time for deliverance and for their circumstances to improve.

Yet the promised time will eventually come.

Before God brought Israel into conflict with its enemies in Canaan, he taught the people to forgive their enemies in Edom.

They were not to use God's covenant or his guidance as an excuse to seize everything they could obtain.

Property rights are not founded simply on possessing God's grace.

Israel would have a suitable place to live, but that did not mean the people could claim the whole earth for themselves.

Religion must never become a disguise for injustice.

Israel did not need to depend upon Edom's generosity; the people had the all-sufficient God to trust.

They were to use what they already possessed wisely and gratefully.

Since God had supplied their needs through Providence, they were never to use crooked methods to obtain more.

These principles also apply to individual believers.

Israel must spare Moab and Ammon (verses 8–23)

The history explains the origins of Moab, Edom and Ammon.

It also reaches back to an even older population movement: the Caphtorites displaced the Avvim from their land.

Such changes show how uncertain earthly property and social position are.

Families lose their estates while other families increase.

Earthly possessions have never remained fixed forever.

These histories were meant to encourage Israel.

If God had given lands to Moab and Ammon through his providence, how much more surely would he fulfill his own promise to Israel!

But the Lord commanded Israel not to fight Moab or Ammon.

We must not wrong others merely because they are wicked.

God gives earthly benefits even to people who do not serve him.

These are not his best blessings.

He has far better gifts in store for his own children.

God gives Israel the Amorites' land (verses 24–37)

God tested Israel by forbidding it to seize the wealthy lands of Moab and Ammon.

Then he gave the people the land of the Amorites.

When we refrain from what God forbids, obedience will not ultimately harm us.

The earth and everything in it belong to the Lord, who distributes its possessions as he wills.

But unless someone receives a clear divine command, that person cannot claim God's authority as an excuse for taking another person's land.

Although God promised the Amorites' territory to Israel, the people still had to fight to take possession of it.

We must exert ourselves to obtain what the Lord gives.

What a different world Israel entered as it approached Canaan!

Still greater will be the change experienced by holy souls when they leave this world's wilderness for the better, heavenly country—the city that has firm foundations.

As we remember Israel's history, let us also remember the years we wasted through our sins.

Happy are those whom Jesus has delivered from the coming judgment and who have received his Spirit as the pledge of their inheritance.

That heavenly inheritance cannot be altered by the rise and fall of kingdoms or by changes in earthly possessions.
classic_reading:
[Deut.2.1-Deut.2.7]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
The Edomites to be spared. | (1-7) |
The Moabites and Ammonites to be spared. | (8-23) |
The Amorites to be destroyed. | (24-37) |
Verses 1-7
Only a short account of the long stay of Israel in the wilderness is given. God not only chastised them for their murmuring and unbelief, but prepared them for Canaan; by humbling them for sin, teaching them to mortify their lusts, to follow God, and to comfort themselves in him. Though Israel may be long kept waiting for deliverance and enlargement, it will come at last. Before God brought Israel to destroy their enemies in Canaan, he taught them to forgive their enemies in Edom. They must not, under pretence of God's covenant and conduct, think to seize all they could lay hands on. Dominion is not founded in grace. God's Israel shall be well placed, but must not expect to be placed alone in the midst of the earth. Religion must never be made a cloak for injustice. Scorn to be beholden to Edomites, when thou hast an all-sufficient God to depend upon. Use what thou hast, use it cheerfully. Thou hast experienced the care of the Divine providence, never use any crooked methods for thy supply. All this is equally to be applied to the experience of the believer.
[Deut.2.8-Deut.2.23]
Verses 8-23
We have the origin of the Moabites, Edomites, and Ammonites. Moses also gives an instance older than any of these; the Caphtorims drove the Avims out of their country. These revolutions show what uncertain things wordly possessions are. It was so of old, and ever will be so. Families decline, and from them estates are transferred to families that increase; so little continuance is there in these things. This is recorded to encourage the children of Israel. If the providence of God has done this for Moabites and Ammonites, much more would his promise do it for Israel, his peculiar people. Cautions are given not to meddle with Moabites and Ammonites. Even wicked men must not be wronged. God gives and preserves outward blessings to wicked men; these are not the best things, he has better in store for his own children.
[Deut.2.24-Deut.2.37]
Verses 24-37
God tried his people, by forbidding them to meddle with the rich countries of Moab and Ammon. He gives them possession of the country of the Amorites. If we keep from what God forbids, we shall not lose by our obedience. The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof; and he gives it to whom he pleases; but when there is no express direction, none can plead his grant for such proceedings. Though God assured the Israelites that the land should be their own, yet they must contend with the enemy. What God gives we must endeavour to get. What a new world did Israel now come into! Much more joyful will the change be, which holy souls will experience, when they remove out of the wilderness of this world to the better country, that is, the heavenly, to the city that has foundations. Let us, by reflecting upon God's dealings with his people Israel, be led to meditate upon our years spent in vanity, through our transgressions. But happy are those whom Jesus has delivered from the wrath to come. To whom he hath given the earnest of his Spirit in their hearts. Their inheritance cannot be affected by revolutions of kingdoms, or changes in earthly possessions.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe conquest of Og king of Bashan.1–11The land of Gilead and Bashan.12–20Moses encourages Joshua.21–29
Og, king of Bashan, is defeated (verses 1–11)

Og was extremely powerful.

Yet he learned nothing from the destruction of Sihon.

He could have sought peace, but he continued trusting in his own strength.

His stubbornness led toward his destruction.

Those whom God's judgments against other sinners fail to awaken become more prepared to receive the same judgments themselves.

The tribes settle east of the Jordan (verses 12–20)

The lands of Gilead and Bashan were assigned to Reuben, Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh (Numbers 32).

Moses repeated the condition these tribes had accepted: they must help their brothers complete the conquest before settling down themselves.

When we have received peace, we should desire peace for others too.

We ought to do what we can to help other people obtain it.

We were not born only for ourselves.

We are members of one another.

Moses encourages Joshua and accepts God's answer (verses 21–29)

Moses strengthened Joshua, who would succeed him.

Older and more experienced believers should do everything they can to encourage younger people beginning to serve God.

Remember what God has done and what he has promised.

If God is for us, who can overcome us?

We dishonor our Leader when we follow him trembling with fear.

Moses prayed that, if it were the Lord's will, he might cross the Jordan and enter Canaan with Israel.

We should not cherish any desire that we cannot honestly present to God in prayer.

The answer Moses received combined mercy and judgment.

God sometimes chooses to deny us what we want.

A prayer can be accepted even though the exact request is not granted.

If God's providence does not give us our desire, but his grace makes us content without it, we have still received a great blessing.

Let it be enough to have God as our Father and heaven as our inheritance, even if we cannot possess everything we would like in this world.

God promised Moses a view of Canaan from the summit of Pisgah.

He would not possess it, but he would see it.

Even great believers now see heaven from a distance.

God also provided a successor for Moses.

Friends of Christ's church can be encouraged that the Lord's work will continue through others after they themselves have died.

If we have the pledge of heaven and can already see its prospect, let us be content with that.

We should submit to the Lord's will and stop insisting on what he has wisely refused.
classic_reading:
[Deut.3.1-Deut.3.11]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The conquest of Og king of Bashan. | (1-11) |
The land of Gilead and Bashan. | (12-20) |
Moses encourages Joshua. | (21-29) |
Verses 1-11
Og was very powerful, but he did not take warning by the ruin of Sihon, and desire conditions of peace. He trusted his own strength, and so was hardened to his destruction. Those not awakened by the judgments of God on others, ripen for the like judgments on themselves.
[Deut.3.12-Deut.3.20]
Verses 12-20
This country was settled on the Reubenites, Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh: see Nu 32. Moses repeats the condition of the grant to which they agreed. When at rest, we should desire to see our brethren at rest too, and should be ready to do what we can towards it; for we are not born for ourselves, but are members one of another.
[Deut.3.21-Deut.3.29]
Verses 21-29
Moses encouraged Joshua, who was to succeed him. Thus the aged and experienced in the service of God, should do all they can to strengthen the hands of those who are young, and setting out in religion. Consider what God has done, what God has promised. If God be for us, who can be against us, so as to prevail? We reproach our Leader if we follow him trembling. Moses prayed, that, if it were God's will, he might go before Israel, over Jordan into Canaan. We should never allow any desires in our hearts, which we cannot in faith offer up to God by prayer. God's answer to this prayer had a mixture of mercy and judgment. God sees it good to deny many things we desire. He may accept our prayers, yet not grant us the very things we pray for. It God does not by his providence give us what we desire, yet if by his grace he makes us content without, it comes to much the same. Let it suffice thee to have God for thy Father, and heaven for thy portion, though thou hast not every thing thou wouldst have in the world. God promised Moses a sight of Canaan from the top of Pisgah. Though he should not have the possession of it, he should have the prospect of it. Even great believers, in this present state, see heaven but at a distance. God provided him a successor. It is a comfort to the friends of the church of Christ, to see God's work likely to be carried on by others, when they are silent in the dust. And if we have the earnest and prospect of heaven, let these suffice us; let us submit to the Lord's will, and speak no more to Him of matters which he sees good to refuse us.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesEarnest exhortations to obedience, and dissuasives from idolatry.1–23Warnings against disobedience, and promises of mercy.24–40Cities of refuge appointed.41–49
Moses urges obedience and warns against idolatry (verses 1–23)

God's power and love toward Israel gave Moses many reasons to warn the people solemnly against sin.

The warnings particularly concerned Israel's national covenant, but they can also be applied to people who live under the gospel.

What purpose does a law serve if not to be obeyed?

Our obedience cannot earn eternal salvation.

But it is the only evidence that we have received God's gift of eternal life through Jesus Christ.

We are surrounded by many temptations, and corrupt desires remain within our hearts.

We therefore need to guard our hearts carefully.

People cannot walk on the right path if they walk carelessly.

Moses warned particularly against idolatry.

Anyone who thinks clearly should see how weak the temptation is.

The supposed gods—the sun, moon and stars—are creatures God has generously given to all nations.

How absurd it is to worship what he created to serve us!

We must take care not to forget the Lord's covenant.

We need vigilance, thoughtfulness and watchfulness to prevent the forgetfulness that would lead us away from faith.

Warnings, mercy and the greatness of God (verses 24–40)

Moses appealed to God's greatness, glory and goodness.

If we truly considered the One to whom we answer, we would take our duty seriously and not dare to sin against him.

Why turn away from a merciful God who will never abandon those who remain faithful to him?

Where else could we go?

May his love and mercy bind us to him.

Moses reminded Israel that God was its sovereign and that the people owed him obedience.

Keeping his commands was also wise for their own sake.

Fear of the Lord is wisdom.

People privileged to receive divine truth and law ought to live honorably and wisely, so that God is glorified.

God hears those who call on him in faith.

He is near enough to answer their prayers with peace.

His laws are just and righteous beyond the laws of other nations.

What Israel saw at Sinai gave a foretaste of the final day of judgment, when the Lord Jesus will be revealed in flaming fire.

The people must also remember what they heard there.

God reveals himself through the works of creation without human language, yet their testimony reaches everywhere (Psalm 19:1, 3).

At Sinai he spoke in words the people could hear, graciously adapting himself to their weakness.

Israel's origin was unlike that of every other nation.

God's free grace explains the distinction.

We are not loved because of some merit in ourselves, but for Christ's sake.

Moses also pointed out the benefits of obedience.

At the beginning of his speech (verse 1), he had said that obedience would enable them to live and enter the land.

At its end (verse 40), he promised that obedience would lead to good for them and their children.

Israel's national prosperity was bound to its faithfulness.

Apostasy would ruin the nation.

Moses foresaw that Israel would turn from the Lord to idols.

Only people who seek God with their whole heart will find him to their lasting comfort.

Afflictions often stir us to seek him, and through God's grace they bring many people back to sound judgment.

When such troubles come, return to the Lord: they show what follows from abandoning him.

Consider all these reasons together, and you will see that faith is entirely reasonable.

People abandon God's rule only after abandoning sound human understanding.

The cities of refuge and the next address (verses 41–49)

This passage introduces another address Moses would give to Israel in the following chapters.

He placed God's law before them.

It was to be the guide for their actions and the way they lived.

It was also to be a mirror in which they recognized their own natural condition.

Looking into this perfect law of liberty, they were to continue in obedience.

The instructions first given after Israel came out of Egypt were now repeated.

Moses gave them while the people were camped opposite Beth-peor, a Moabite center of idolatry.

Israel's recent victories offered another strong reason to obey God.

We should similarly understand our own condition as sinners and the gracious covenant to which we are invited.

That covenant reveals greater things than Israel witnessed at Sinai and provides mercies beyond what the people enjoyed in the wilderness or Canaan.

The One who speaks to us is infinitely greater than Moses.

He bore our sins on the cross and appeals to us through his dying love.
classic_reading:
[Deut.4.1-Deut.4.23]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
Earnest exhortations to obedience, and dissuasives from idolatry. | (1-23) |
Warnings against disobedience, and promises of mercy. | (24-40) |
Cities of refuge appointed. | (41-49) |
Verses 1-23
The power and love of God to Israel are here made the ground and reason of a number of cautions and serious warnings; and although there is much reference to their national covenant, yet all may be applied to those who live under the gospel. What are laws made for but to be observed and obeyed? Our obedience as individuals cannot merit salvation; but it is the only evidence that we are partakers of the gift of God, which is eternal life through Jesus Christ, Considering how many temptations we are compassed with, and what corrupt desires we have in our bosoms, we have great need to keep our hearts with all diligence. Those cannot walk aright, who walk carelessly. Moses charges particularly to take heed of the sin of idolatry. He shows how weak the temptation would be to those who thought aright; for these pretended gods, the sun, moon, and stars, were only blessings which the Lord their God had imparted to all nations. It is absurd to worship them; shall we serve those that were made to serve us? Take heed lest ye forget the covenant of the Lord your God. We must take heed lest at any time we forget our religion. Care, caution, and watchfulness, are helps against a bad memory.
[Deut.4.24-Deut.4.40]
Verses 24-40
Moses urged the greatness, glory, and goodness of God. Did we consider what a God he is with whom we have to do, we should surely make conscience of our duty to him, and not dare to sin against him. Shall we forsake a merciful God, who will never forsake us, if we are faithful unto him? Whither can we go? Let us be held to our duty by the bonds of love, and prevailed with by the mercies of God to cleave to him. Moses urged God's authority over them, and their obligations to him. In keeping God's commandments they would act wisely for themselves. The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom. Those who enjoy the benefit of Divine light and laws, ought to support their character for wisdom and honour, that God may be glorified thereby. Those who call upon God, shall certainly find him within call, ready to give an answer of peace to every prayer of faith. All these statutes and judgments of the Divine law are just and righteous, above the statutes and judgments of any of the nations. What they saw at mount Sinai, gave an earnest of the day of judgment, in which the Lord Jesus shall be revealed in flaming fire. They must also remember what they heard at mount Sinai. God manifests himself in the works of the creation, without speech or language, yet their voice is heard, [Ps.19.1] Psa 19:1, [Ps.19.3] 3; but to Israel he made himself known by speech and language, condescending to their weakness. The rise of this nation was quite different from the origin of all other nations. See the reasons of free grace; we are not beloved for our own sakes, but for Christ's sake. Moses urged the certain benefit and advantage of obedience. This argument he had begun with, ver. #(1), That ye may live, and go in and possess the land; and this he concludes with, ver. #(40), That it may go well with thee, and with thy children after thee. He reminds them that their prosperity would depend upon their piety. Apostacy from God would undoubtedly be the ruin of their nation. He foresees their revolt from God to idols. Those, and those only, shall find God to their comfort, who seek him with all their heart. Afflictions engage and quicken us to seek God; and, by the grace of God working with them, many are thus brought back to their right mind. When these things are come upon thee, turn to the Lord thy God, for thou seest what comes of turning from him. Let all the arguments be laid together, and then say, if religion has not reason on its side. None cast off the government of their God, but those who first abandon the understanding of a man.
[Deut.4.41-Deut.4.49]
Verses 41-49
Here is the introduction to another discourse, or sermon, Moses preached to Israel, which we have in the following chapters. He sets the law before them, as the rule they were to work by, the way they were to walk in. He sets it before them, as the glass in which they were to see their natural face, that, looking into this perfect law of liberty, they might continue therein. These are the laws, given when Israel was newly come out of Egypt; and they were now repeated. Moses gave these laws in charge, while they encamped over against Beth-peor, an idol place of the Moabites. Their present triumphs were a powerful argument for obedience. And we should understand our own situation as sinners, and the nature of that gracious covenant to which we are invited. Therein greater things are shown to us than ever Israel saw from mount Sinai; greater mercies are given to us than they experienced in the wilderness, or in Canaan. One speaks to us, who is of infinitely greater dignity than Moses; who bare our sins upon the cross; and pleads with us by His dying love.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe covenant in Horeb.1–5The ten commandments repeated.6–22The request of the people that the law might be delivered through Moses.23–33
Israel is called to hear and obey (verses 1–5)

Moses urged Israel to pay attention.

When we hear God's word, we must learn it.

Once we have learned it, we must put it into practice.

That is the purpose of listening and learning.

We are not meant merely to fill our heads with religious information or our mouths with talk.

God's word should direct our affections and conduct.

The Ten Commandments are repeated (verses 6–22)

This account of the commandments differs in some wording from Exodus 20.

Henry compares that difference with the variations between the Lord's Prayer recorded in Matthew 6 and Luke 11.

We must care more about faithfully receiving the truths and commands than about insisting that every repeated account use identical words.

The original reason for observing the Sabbath—the Lord's rest after creating the world on the seventh day—is not mentioned here.

That reason remains valid, but it is not the only one.

Here Moses appeals to Israel's deliverance from Egypt.

That deliverance pointed to our redemption through Jesus Christ.

Henry connects it with the Christian Sabbath, which remembers that redemption.

Through Christ's resurrection we were brought into the glorious freedom of God's children, by his strong hand and outstretched arm.

How gentle and life-giving the gospel sounds to a soul burdened by the terrors of a broken law!

The people ask Moses to speak for them (verses 23–33)

Moses recalled how terrified the people had been when God gave the law.

Ever since humanity's fall, divine appearances have been frightening to guilty people.

But Christ has removed sin, and through him we are invited to approach the throne of grace boldly.

The people seemed sincere while they were deeply convicted by the word they had heard.

Yet conscience can be alarmed by the law without becoming clean.

Strong feelings may force people to make excellent promises without creating new and lasting principles within them.

God commended the words Israel spoke.

He truly desires the good and salvation of sinners.

He has supplied abundant evidence.

He gives people time and opportunity to repent.

He sent his Son to redeem us, promised the Spirit to those who ask, and declared that he takes no pleasure in sinners' destruction.

How good it would be if people always had the hearts they sometimes seem to have under conviction, painful providence or the approach of death.

The only way to be truly happy is to become holy.

It will go well with the righteous.

Believers should increasingly delight in learning and doing everything the Lord has commanded.
classic_reading:
[Deut.5.1-Deut.5.5]
Chapter 5
Chapter Outline
The covenant in Horeb. | (1-5) |
The ten commandments repeated. | (6-22) |
The request of the people that the law might be delivered through Moses. | (23-33) |
Verses 1-5
Moses demands attention. When we hear the word of God we must learn it; and what we have learned we must put in practice, for that is the end of hearing and learning; not to fill our heads with notions, or our mouths with talk, but to direct our affections and conduct.
[Deut.5.6-Deut.5.22]
Verses 6-22
There is some variation here from Ex 20 as between the Lord's prayer in Mt 6 and Lu 11. It is more necessary that we tie ourselves to the things, than to the words unalterably. The original reason for hallowing the sabbath, taken from God's resting from the work of creation on the seventh day, is not here mentioned. Though this ever remains in force, it is not the only reason. Here it is taken from Israel's deliverance out of Egypt; for that was typical of our redemption by Jesus Christ, in remembrance of which the Christian sabbath was to be observed. In the resurrection of Christ we were brought into the glorious liberty of the children of God, with a mighty hand, and an outstretched arm. We must walk in the ways in which he has appointed us to walk. We must serve him with all our heart and soul. What we do in his service we must do cheerfully, and with good will. We must keep his commandments. There is true honour and pleasure in obedience. We must give honour to God; and to him we must cleave, as one we love and delight in, trust in, and from whom we have great expectations. We are here taught our duty to our neighbour. God's common gifts to mankind oblige us to honour all men. And those who have themselves been in distress, and have found mercy with God, should be ready to show kindness to those who are in the like distress. We are here taught our duty to ourselves. Circumcise your hearts. Cast away all corrupt affections and inclinations, which hinder you from fearing and loving God. By nature we do not love God. This is original sin, the source whence our wickedness proceeds; and the carnal mind is enmity against God, for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be; so then they that are in the flesh cannot please God, [Rom.8.5-Rom.8.9] Ro 8:5-9. Let us, without delay or reserve, come and cleave to our reconciled God in Jesus Christ, that we may love, serve, and obey him acceptably, and be daily changed into his image, from glory to glory, by the Spirit of the Lord. Consider the greatness and glory of God; and his goodness and grace; these persuade us to our duty. Blessed Spirit! Oh for thy purifying, persevering, and renewing influences, that being called out of the state of strangers, such as our fathers were, we may be found among the number of the children of God, and that our lot may be among the saints.
